subtopic_detail: Methotrexate versus surgery for tubal ectopic
stem:
A 28-year-old nulligravid woman presents to an early pregnancy assessment service with 3 days of intermittent left iliac fossa pain and light brown vaginal spotting. Her last menstrual period was 6 weeks and 4 days ago and she confirmed pregnancy on a home test 2 weeks ago. She is haemodynamically stable, well perfused, has minimal focal tenderness on abdominal palpation, and is not distressed.

A transvaginal ultrasound today shows an empty uterine cavity with a 12 mm endometrium, an unruptured left tubal mass of 28 mm without embryonic cardiac activity, and no significant free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. Serum beta hCG this morning is 4200 IU/L (48 hour rise ceased). She is a reliable follow-up attendee, has no active liver, renal or haematological disease, and is not breastfeeding. She has a strong preference to avoid surgery if possible.

data_table.Investigations: beta hCG 4200 IU/L, haemoglobin 128 g/L (115-165), platelets 240 x10 to the 9 per litre (150-400), alanine aminotransferase 22 U/L (less than 35), creatinine 60 micromol/L (45-90), blood group O rhesus positive
data_table.Imaging: transvaginal ultrasound with empty uterus, left tubal mass 28 mm without cardiac activity, no free fluid

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Proceed to urgent laparoscopic left salpingectomy under general anaesthesia within the next operating theatre list
options.rationale: Surgical management is required for beta hCG at or above 5000 IU/L, ruptured ectopic, haemodynamic instability, or contraindications to methotrexate. None apply here. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 61 Ectopic Pregnancy)

options.text: Repeat the beta hCG in 48 hours and defer treatment until a further rise or fall is confirmed on trend
options.rationale: The diagnosis of tubal ectopic is already made on ultrasound with a plateaued beta hCG. Deferring treatment for another 48 hours risks rupture. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 61 Ectopic Pregnancy)

options.text: Administer a single dose intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg/m2 with weekly serum beta hCG surveillance to resolution
options.rationale: RANZCOG allows methotrexate for a tubal ectopic when beta hCG is under 5000 IU/L, the mass is under 3.5 cm, no cardiac activity is present, pain is minimal, follow-up is reliable, and there are no medical contraindications. All criteria are met here. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 61 Ectopic Pregnancy)

options.text: Commence expectant management with weekly clinical and biochemical review until spontaneous resolution occurs
options.rationale: Expectant management is confined to a very low and falling beta hCG (typically under 1500 IU/L and declining). At 4200 IU/L it is not appropriate. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 61 Ectopic Pregnancy)

options.text: Administer a course of mifepristone with misoprostol as a medical evacuation of the uterine pregnancy retained
options.rationale: Mifepristone-misoprostol is for intrauterine pregnancy and has no role in tubal ectopic. It does not resolve tubal implantation. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 61 Ectopic Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: This unruptured tubal ectopic meets every RANZCOG criterion for medical management: beta hCG under 5000 IU/L, mass under 3.5 cm, no cardiac activity, minimal pain, reliable follow-up, and no medical contraindications. Single dose methotrexate 50 mg/m2 IM with weekly hCG surveillance is appropriate. Surgery is reserved for higher hCG, rupture, or failure of methotrexate.
key_points: RANZCOG methotrexate criteria: hCG under 5000, mass under 3.5 cm, no cardiac activity, minimal pain, reliable follow-up, no MTX contraindications
Surgical management indicated if any criterion is unmet or rupture is suspected
Weekly hCG until under 5 IU/L is the AU surveillance protocol
explanation.pearls: The AU hCG surgical cut-off is 5000 IU/L, not 3000. This is a common misremember.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Ectopic pregnancy medical management
